overview: Pomeranian culture developed during the Early Iron Age in northern Poland and spread into other regions. Its face-decorated burial urns are especially recognizable. These were communities sharing practices, not one known kingdom. The map’s narrow northern outline misses much of their wider distribution, and its 200 CE endpoint extends too late.

periods.title: Face urns and regional traditions
periods.summary: Northern communities developed distinctive vessels and burial arrangements.

periods.title: Wider contacts and change
periods.summary: Practices spread and mixed with other regional traditions before later archaeological cultures emerged.

items.text: Pomeranian communities lived in small open settlements with houses supported by wooden posts. Farming included wheat, barley and rye, alongside livestock keeping. The museum synthesis describes flexible use of lighter soils, reminding us that everyday life involved fields and animals as well as elaborate graves.

A wooden ard from Lisie Jamy survives in Gdańsk’s collection. Dated broadly to the Early Iron Age, it shows the sort of soil-working equipment used in this regional world. Wood usually decays, so such a tool supplies evidence that metal objects alone would miss.

A hoard from Rekowo contains bronze axes and ankle ornaments, catalogued as Pomeranian and dated broadly between 700 and 400 BCE. Tools and dress ornaments required skilled metalworking. The hoard groups useful and decorative objects together, without preserving its owner’s reason for depositing them.

A face urn from Gościcino is dated about 550 to 400 BCE. Its human features belong to a vessel made to hold cremated remains. These striking pots put a face into the archaeological record, but that does not make them reliable portraits of particular individuals.

Researchers once tried sorting face urns into male and female examples by deciding which faces were prettier. Gdańsk’s museum explains that anthropological study undermined that approach. Archaeology improves when an appealing assumption is tested against the actual remains.

Face urns could show people, animals and horse teams. Their origins are debated: proposed connections include Etruscan vessels in Italy and earlier eye-decorated urns farther north. Similarity provides a question to investigate; it does not by itself establish one migration or a shared identity.

Some graves were chambers built from stone slabs, with gaps filled by rubble and clay and a large stone above. They could hold several urns or more than a dozen. Constructing and revisiting such a burial place required practical work as well as mourning.

The Poznań exhibition describes cist graves receiving additional burials over generations. This gives a picture of repeated family remembrance rather than every funeral creating a completely separate monument. Archaeologists still need evidence from the remains before reconstructing particular biological relationships.

Urns sometimes carry hunting scenes or pictures of pins, shields and spears. Such designs preserve recognizable equipment and activities. The drawing is evidence of what people chose to depict, rather than a complete inventory of what each household owned.

Bird images occur only occasionally on Pomeranian pottery and other objects in the Poznań exhibition. Their relative scarcity is worth recording, but it does not tell us how often people watched birds, told stories about them or heard them around their settlements.

The Chojnice exhibition brings together bronze jewellery, tools and grooming implements alongside urns. These objects connect the funerary evidence with dressing and caring for the body. An ancient person’s possessions could include practical personal equipment as well as conspicuous ornaments.

The images on these urns are not securely deciphered sentences. No writing sample in the makers’ own language is established by the sources used here. A picture of jewellery can tell us something about appearance while leaving the wearer’s name and spoken words unknown.

ending.text: By the later third century BCE, archaeological patterns associated with Przeworsk and Oksywie replaced Pomeranian traditions in different areas. This is not a recorded conquest of one state. People and practices changed, while the map’s extension to 200 CE misleadingly prolongs the label.
